newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela phone company share issue gets good start.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela phone company share issue gets good start.

text.p: Venezuelan truck driver Antonio Mantilla, one of 50,000 small Venezuelan investors, feels he will be earning rather than spending every time he uses his telephone.
Mantilla is seeking to buy a stake in national telephone company CANTV, and like the other investors, had until Friday to do so.
"It's the only real telephone company in the country, it's well run, and it has a great future," he said as he waited in a long line outside a Caracas bank to place order for shares.

Mantilla was able to buy shares under a plan that earmarked 50 million shares for the local market in the global 239 million share offering -- one of the largest to come out of Latin America this year.
Institutional Venezuelan investors can place orders Monday and Tuesday next week.
The reference price ranged from $3.07 to $3.50, although the final price could be higher when it is settled on November 21. CANTV shares will begin to trade at the end of the month.

The share issue is for 40 percent of the government's remaining 49 percent stake in CANTV. Nine percent will be offered to workers. A controlling 40 percent stake was sold in 1991 to a consortium led by GTE Corp of the United States.
"We're very pleased at how people have responded," said Agustin Cangas, president of Merinvest, one of the local lead syndicates.
He said demand had crescendoed through the week after a slow start. "Venezuelans always come through at the last moment, in the last hour, on the last day," he said.

But despite the hurry, Venezuelans have managed to place orders for some $105 million worth of shares, according to official figures, with demand particularly strong in the capital Caracas which enjoys a stronger financial culture.
"The prospectuses arrived late ... so did the share order forms, but nevertheless it's all gone well," one broker said.

"In other countries a privatisation such as this would have had six months' preparation. But here they had to change legislation, get congressional authorisation, and that all took up a lot of time," another broker, Jose Gregorio Tineo, said.

The share placement, seen by analysts as a litmus test of Venezuelan commitment to tough economic reforms implemented under the International Monetary Fund's guidance, is expected to send the Caracas bolsa for a loop.

Traders see CANTV shares displacing current market leader Electricidad de Caracas from its top slot, and boosting market capitalisation from present levels of 3.6 trillion bolivars ($7.73 billion), according to stock exchange figures.
"It will completely change the bolsa and the attitude of Venezuelans towards savings and risk," said Caracas bolsa President Alejandro Salcedo.
He said it would also ready the bolsa for other large, expected initial public offerings.
State-owned holding company Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana is due to privatise its steel and aluminium producing arms early next year, with some 10 percent of shares reserved for the bolsa.
Some see the boom more than doubling the Caracas bolsa's index by the end of 1997 to around 14,000.00 points. On Friday the index closed at 5,966.75.
